title: CLOSING BELL: Bathla hasn't scared ART off private credit
full_text:
Ian Patrick, chief investment officer of the $370 billion superannuation giant Australian Retirement Trust, never thought he would need to become a pest inspector. But private credit changed that.
ART has a $10 billion exposure to private credit, and as scrutiny on the sector has grown over the past 12 months, ART's investment committee has asked Patrick and his team to look closely at the health of those investments in Australia and the US.
"When somebody like [JPMorgan CEO] Jamie Dimon says there are cockroaches [in private credit], the first question anybody asks is, 'Have I got any in my kitchen?"' says ART's chief investment officer.
"It's one thing to make the initial commitment. But it's still incumbent on us to go through the re-underwriting, let's call it, of both the manager and the exposures in their portfolio," says Patrick, who will appear at The Australian Financial Review Super and Wealth Summit in Melbourne on Monday.
Dimon's comments followed the spectacular implosion of two US firms, a subprime auto sector lender called Tricolor, and a car parts group called First Brands.
Scrutiny on the private credit sector intensified early this year as disruption from artificial intelligence threatened the global software-as-a-service sector - about 30 per cent of all private credit loans were to SaaS players.
In Australia, the corporate regulator has also been stepping up its supervision of local private credit players over the past two years, raising important questions about industry standards and concentration in property lending.
When Western Sydney home builder Bathla went under in August with about $3 billion of debt from private credit lenders, it appeared Dimon's cockroaches had crossed the Pacific.
ART had a $22 million exposure to Bathla via its investments in a private credit fund run by Asian financial services giant PAG.
So over the past few months, Patrick has donned the rubber gloves and shone the torch in dark places. His verdict? Private credit's fundamentals are actually pretty solid - but it's clearly got an image problem.
About 90 per cent of ART's private credit exposure is global funds that invest across a wide variety of geographies, sectors and companies; where private credit is heavily concentrated in property in Australia, Patrick says ART sees its own private credit portfolio as strongly diversified.
Yes, there has been an increase in private credit defaults; according to the latest numbers from ratings agency Fitch, the US default rate hit a record high of 6.3 per cent in August, up from 5.2 per cent a year earlier.
But Patrick says he is not seeing anything inside the portfolio of ART and its external managers that suggests disaster is approaching.
"Whilst defaults have ticked up a tiny bit around the world, they're well within the concept of a credit cycle, and so we're not seeing any particular issue," he says. "There's been some hyperventilating, but institutional portfolios are in reasonably good or very good shape."
In addition to reviewing both the private credit managers ART works with and its individual exposures, ART's separate valuations team has examined how private credit exposures have been marked.
"We're particularly pleased with the discipline on valuations that we're seeing in our managers," says Patrick.
The other piece of the puzzle that doesn't get as much attention is returns, which Patrick says have held up well, at about 1.5 per cent to 2 per cent above high-yield debt returns and leveraged loans. That suggests a yield of 10 per cent to 10.5 per cent.
Which brings us to Bathla - a chastening experience for Australia's private credit sector - and another signal for ART to review its exposures.
The first point, Patrick says, is the episode has served as a valuable reminder that there is a good reason why Australia only counts for 10 per cent of ART's private credit exposure. The market is relatively small and relatively concentrated. Because the banking sector is strong here, private credit ends up focusing on areas where the banks do not want to tread, especially property.
That leads to the second key point. Yes, ART is thinking hard about its overall exposure to Australian property, given, for example, its Australian equities portfolio contains a good amount of shares in the big four banks, which write a bucket load of mortgages. ART's whole-of-portfolio exposure to Australian residential property is another reason to be careful about its local private credit holdings.
Third, Patrick says he is satisfied there is a way out of the Bathla mess for PAG and ART.
"Clearly you don't want the default in the first place, but having said that, it is well within the bounds of what we have planned for," he says.
"Every indication we have, having gone into this in depth with PAG, is that recoveries are anticipated to be really, really high [and] impairment of capital is a very, very low probability, although we may not get the full level of return that was originally underwritten."
So if Patrick is still a private credit believer, does the run of poor headlines in the sector provide a chance for the fund to play the contrarian and increase its private credit exposure at attractive prices?
Patrick is cautious. ART thinks of private credit as a mid-risk asset class, alongside infrastructure and real estate.
Right now, the CIO says, with the prospect that higher borrowing costs and AI disruption do cause a bit more stress, ART is neutral on the sector; it wouldn't reduce its allocation, but it won't be rushing to increase it, either.
"In other words, private credit is robust, but it's not a screaming buy relative to the other two," says Patrick.
